title: Quantum-Enabled Spintronic "Small" Antennas
abstract: Antennas transmit information wirelessly from one location to another via electromagnetic waves. Miniaturizing them, however, is challenging since the radiation efficiencies of all traditional antennas, based on the principles of classical electromagnetics, plummet when their dimensions are shrunk to tiny fractions of the radiated wavelength. Lately, a new generation of antennas whose operations are underpinned by non-classical principles have been demonstrated and they can overcome this limitation. This enables embedded applications that were hitherto inaccessible. In addition, beam steering, which normally requires a large phased array (multiple antenna elements each much larger than the wavelength), can now be accomplished with a single element much smaller than the wavelength. Some of these antennas also have stealth attributes for secure and covert communication, which makes this new genre a disruptive new technology.
summary: The paper introduces quantum-enabled spintronic antennas that overcome the size limitations of traditional antennas by utilizing artificial multiferroic magnonic crystals. By coupling phonons (from acoustic waves) to magnons and subsequently to photons, these structures achieve radiation efficiencies orders of magnitude higher than classical predictions. This breakthrough enables highly miniaturized devices for applications like medical implants and covert communication.
main_problem: Traditional antennas fail to maintain high radiation efficiency when miniaturized below fractions of the radiated wavelength due to classical electromagnetic limitations (Harrington limit).
main_result: The use of nanomagnets in magneto-elastic structures successfully generates strong, highly efficient electromagnetic emission from extreme sub-wavelength antennas, significantly exceeding conventional theoretical limits.
method: Measurements involve analyzing radiation efficiency ($\eta = 	ext{Rrad} / (	ext{Rrad} + 	ext{Rloss})$) by comparing samples with and without nanomagnets, alongside characterizing resonant coupling via $S_{11}$ spectra measurements.
model_or_system: The system is an Artificial Multiferroic Magnonic Crystal (AMMC), comprising a 2D periodic array of nanomagnets deposited on a piezoelectric substrate. Energy transfer relies on tripartite phonon-magnon-photon coupling, exciting hybrid magneto-dynamical modes.
key_observables: Radiation efficiency ($\eta$), $S_{11}$ spectra dips indicating resonant energy transfer, and measured receiving gain ($G_r$).
important_parameters: The Harrington limit ($\eta \propto (A/\lambda)^2$); the acoustic wavelength ($\lambda_{	ext{ac}}$) which can be much smaller than the electromagnetic wavelength ($\lambda_{	ext{EM}}$).
main_assumptions: The efficiency enhancement is attributed to utilizing acoustic resonances and non-classical coupling mechanisms, rather than classical magnetic dipole radiation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate theoretical limitations (dipole formation), basic magneto-elastic principles, the nanomagnet array structure, and experimental results showing signal presence only with nanomagnets at various frequencies.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the miniaturization challenge to proposing the AMMC system, detailing the underlying physics of phonon-magnon-photon coupling, presenting measurements confirming resonant enhancement, and finally discussing advanced applications like beam steering and stealth communication.
why_interesting: This work demonstrates how engineered material couplings (phonon/magnon) can circumvent fundamental classical electromagnetic limits to achieve highly efficient energy radiation from nanoscale devices, which is a key concept in open quantum systems and quantum optics applied to solid-state physics.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) A dipole antenna that is one wavelength long and can host a resonant electric dipole. (b) An antenna much smaller than the wavelength cannot host a dipole.

Figure 2: A bulk magnetostrictive magnet on a piezoelectic substrate or film will radiate electromagnetric waves if a surface acoustic wave (SAW) [or a bulk acoustic wave] is launched in the piezoelectric. The acoustic wave generates time varying strain in the magnet and that causes the magnetization to precess because of the inverse magnetostriction (or Villari) effect. The time-varying magnetization radiates electromagnetic waves and this is the basis of a magneto-elastic antenna.

Figure 3: A two-dimensional periodic array of slightly elliptical magnetostrictive nanomagnets deposited on a piezoelectric substrate (or a piezoelectric thin film) forming an “artificial multiferroic magnonic crystal”. A surface acoustic wave launched in the piezoelectric with appropriate electrodes (not shown) will subject the nanomagnets to periodic strain and cause their magnetizations to precess owing to the inverse magne- tostriction effect. This will radiate electromagnetic waves in the surrounding space.

Figure 4: (a) Scanning electron micrograph of a two-dimensional periodic array of nanomagnets deposited on a piezoelectric LiNbO3 substrate in which a RF frequency SAW was launched with electrodes. (b) Higher resolution image showing the nanomagnet dimension and inter-nanomagnet spacing. The nanomagnets are elliptical with major axis dimension ∼360 nm, minor axis ∼330 nm, edge-to-edge spacing ∼65 nm along the major axis direction and ∼42 nm along the minor axis direction. The thickness of the nanomagnets was 6 nm. Reproduced from [17] with CC-BY license.

Figure 5: Electromagnetic radiation spectrum of the real and control samples at 144 MHz and 900 MHz. Two real samples A and B were measured along with their corresponding control samples that contained no nanomagnets. (a) Radiation spectra of the two samples A and B along with those of the corresponding control samples at 144 MHz input SAW frequency. (b) The radiation from a real sample and the corresponding control sample cannot be resolved at 900 MHz input SAW frequency indicating that the nanomagnets are not radiating sufficiently. Spintronics.note: The core mechanism described—energy transfer via phonon-magnon-photon coupling in a multiferroic structure to achieve highly efficient emission—directly falls under the scope of magnon/photon polaritons and hybrid spin-photon systems.
